The exhibition is part of a University of Maryland Arts for All-funded project aimed at engaging students in science communication through art, increasing awareness of insect biodiversity and ecological roles, fostering collaboration across disciplines, evaluating changes in attendee knowledge, attitudes, and intentions, and contributing to a replicable arts-based model for conservation education. The exhibition will highlight six Maryland insect species that are included on Maryland’s List of Rare, Threatened, and Endangered Animals . Original works created through the exhibition’s two different open calls will be displayed alongside science-based information about insect ecological roles, insect habitats, and key conservation actions. events.title: Bison: Standing Strong
events.address: 10th St. & Constitution Ave., NW, Washington, DC 20560
events.description: Explore the remarkable story of bison. These iconic animals shaped North American landscapes for more than 100,000 years and anchored Indigenous lifeways for generations. Pushed to the brink of extinction in the 19th century, bison survived thanks to dedicated conservation efforts. Today, they stand strong as an enduring symbol of survival and resilience. The Bison: Standing Strong exhibit invites you into this incredible journey. Explore a full-sized bull bison specimen, the six-foot-wide skull of an ancient bison ancestor, an immersive soundscape, multimedia, cutting-edge scientific research, and Native objects and stories shared in collaboration with community members. Experience the deep history of America’s national mammal and discover the hopeful future being built for generations to come.

events.title: Bronze Bison: Exhibit
events.address: 10th St. & Constitution Ave., NW, Washington, DC 20560
events.description: More than 100 years ago, real bison grazed outside the Smithsonian Castle building. Bison are returning in a bold new way! Three larger-than-life bronze bison, created by sculptor Gary Staab, find a permanent home outside the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History. These towering sculptures of a bull, cow, and calf are at 125 percent scale and modeled after taxidermy specimens seen at the Smithsonian between 1888 and 1957. The original bison diorama introduced generations of visitors to an animal and a prairie landscape they had never seen and helped spark the bison conservation movement. The new bison bronzes will welcome visitors from around the world and celebrate America’s national mammal. Gift of Naoma Tate and the family of Hal Tate.

events.title: Civil War History in Oakton and Vienna
events.description: Greater Oakton Community Association invites history enthusiasts to join a narrated historic bus tour led by acclaimed local historian Jim Lewis on from 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. Please arrive at 9:00 a.m. at Oakton Community Park at 2841 Hunter Mill Road (next to the old schoolhouse and roundabout) for Jim Lewis's opening comments, then board the bus for departure by 9:30 a.m. The tour will end at 1:00 p.m. This 3.5-hour journey spans Fairfax County's history from its formation in 1742 through the early 1900s, focusing on sites primarily on or just off Hunter Mill Road. Participants hear stories of where the old mills and roads were located and learn about famed military figures (particularly from the Civil War era) and colorful residents who graced the area. Numerous period photographs support the narrative, bringing history to life. Walking requirements are minimal, although one segment involves going down a slight grassy decline. The tour runs rain or shine. Snacks and water are included. Cost is $45 per seat. In the event of cancellation, refunds are provided if a replacement is found for the seat; a wait list is maintained for this purpose. There are 23 seats on the bus. Special "Event Pricing" is offered for the award-winning "Danger Between the Lines" DVD and tour-related illustrated books, available for purchase with cash only. Narrated Historic Bus Tour with Jim Lewis combines local history education, community connection, and immersive storytelling in Fairfax County, Virginia. Questions? Email contact@greateroakton.com . events.title: Entertainment Nation
events.address: 14th Street and Constitution Avenue, N.W., Washington, DC 20560
events.description: Entertainment has the power to captivate, inspire and transform us. It brings us together. We share it when we spontaneously recite lines from a favorite movie, dance to the same groove or recreate a national sports moment on a neighborhood street. It can also spur critical conversations, expose divides, and foster important historical change. Through the National Museum of American History’s extraordinary collection of theater, music, sports, movie and television objects, the exhibition features a powerful, ever-changing selection of objects and interactive experiences. Through the objects and their stories, the exhibition explores how, for more than 150 years, entertainment has provided a forum for important national conversations about who we are, and who we want to be.

events.title: Friends Gather Here: A Legacy of Two Communities at Woodlawn
events.description: Friends Gather Here: A Legacy of Two Communities at Woodlawn explores the powerful history of Quaker families who came to Woodlawn to establish an antislavery community rooted in equality and nonviolence. Through innovative farming and free labor, they sought to demonstrate an alternative to slavery in Virginia, settling alongside a small, established free Black community already living in the area. This exhibit examines the parallel lives, shared aspirations, and evolving relationships between these neighboring communities. As part of the Virginia 250th commemoration, Friends Gather Here invites us to reflect on this quiet revolution and examine our nation’s foundational ideals. On View: June 27 – December 30, 2026 Admission: Free (with suggested donation)

events.title: GlySpace Alliance Webinar
events.description: Agentic Curation of the PathophysiomePresented by: Chris Mungall, PhD Senior Computer Scientist, Biosystems Data Science, Berkeley Lab Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory Chris Mungall, PhD is a Staff Scientist in the Environmental Genomics and Systems Biology Division at LBNL, where he heads the Biosystems Data Science department. Chris’s research interests center around the capture, computational integration, and dissemination of biological research data, and the development of methods for using this data to elucidate biological mechanisms underpinning the health of humans and of the planet. He and his team have led the creation of key biological ontologies for the integration of resources covering gene function, anatomy, phenotypes and the environment. In the Gene Ontology project and others, Chris and his collaborators develop systems that help curators translate biological knowledge into a computable form, and apply that biological knowledge to answer complex biological questions. Abstract: DisMech is a knowledge base that connects molecular defects to disease phenotypes through structured, literature and analysis supported mechanisms. I’ll describe how AI agents curate and review this knowledge, supported by automated checks of schemas, ontology terms, and quoted evidence. Examples from congenital disorders of glycosylation will illustrate the approach and open a discussion of how GlyGen could help connect genes, altered glycoproteins, and clinical outcomes. WhereVirt

events.title: In Pursuit of Life, Liberty & Happiness
events.address: 14th Street and Constitution Avenue, N.W., Washington, DC 20560
events.description: The Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History will lead the nation’s 250th anniversary celebrations with a bold, immersive exhibition exploring the ideals of the Declaration of Independence. In Pursuit of Life, Liberty & Happiness will span three floors and 300,000 square feet, featuring 250 significant objects, including the desk Jefferson used to draft the Declaration of Independence. Another noteworthy artifact is the only surviving ship of the early U.S. Navy, the gunboat Philadelphia . This National Historic Landmark helped stall British forces and now will undergo an on-site conservation to preserve it for future generations. Visitors and online audiences can engage with both the triumphs and challenges of America’s journey through a year-long series of dynamic programs, from hands-on activities and theatrical performances to educational tools and virtual field trips for classrooms across the country. The museum's Semiquincentennial exhibitions and events begin in the spring of 2026, welcoming all Americans to reflect on the enduring and sometimes delayed or denied promises that surround the ongoing pursuit of life, liberty and happiness.

events.title: Leech Woods
events.address: 11201 Bethesda Church Road, Damascus View, Diamond View
events.description: Welcome to L eech Woods According to Montgomery County historical land records, the present site of Leech Woods was originally settled by Warwick and Jeanne Leech and their six children sometime in early 1790. Having immigrated from Hungary, the family chose Damascus, Maryland, based on its temperate climate and heavily wooded region, which reminded them of their homeland. The Leech family store thrived as the leading local merchant of hides, furs, and hunting supplies. During the disastrous Winter of 1804, the Leech family store was robbed and vandalized by unknown attackers and the body of John Leech, the youngest son, was found nailed to the back wall of the store. The remaining bodies of the family members were later found bludgeoned and bound inside of the root cellar of their homestead. No further information about the attackers or motives for the killings is known. ​ Remnants of the Leech family homestead still stand deep in the woods where the present Leech Woods experience is built. The Leech Woods immersive experience follows the original walking path from the site of the Leech family hunting supply store to the remnants of the original family homestead. As the property was classified as a historical site in 1972, no artifacts may be removed, and we ask that you respect the privacy of the grave sites. What’s new? More Scares. More scenes. events.title: Mary Grueso Romero: A Talk with the Poet of the Pacific
events.description: Mary Grueso Romero, "The Poet of the Pacific", is a celebrated Afro-Colombian writer and educator and the first Afro-Colombian woman inducted into the Colombian Academy of the Spanish Language. She was born in 1947 in Chuare Napi village, Guapi, Cauca Department, Colombia, known for being an afro enclave with a long history of music and oral storytelling. She worked as a teacher for more than thirty years and in 2010 Grueso was recognised as the best teacher in Valle del Cauca thanks to her project using literature to empower Afro-Colombian students. While working as a teacher Grueso also wrote children's stories, whose protagonists and narratives were typical of the Afro-Colombian culture of the Pacific coast of Colombia. Her style is characterised by an oral rhythm and musicality of language, with the use of Afro-Colombian expressions, the recovery of ancestral knowledge from communities in a natural setting, and recurring themes such as black women, community and song. She has also participated in national and international festivals as an oral storyteller. Her children's book La muñeca negra (transl. The Black Doll) became her main bestseller.

events.title: Miguel Braceli: UNBURIAL (exhibition)
events.address: St. John's College, 60 College Avenue, Annapolis, MD 21401
events.description: Unburial treats absence as a site for learning and reflection. The void left by the Liberty Tree becomes more than metaphor: an art intervention transforms it into a place to be repurposed and reclaimed through rituals and celebrations that probe what freedom means today. On the front lawn, where the Liberty Tree once stood, the artist Miguel Braceli has installed a 40'-diameter circle of cemetery vases filled with common wildflowers. It calls attention to the tree's absence and reclaims it as a tree for all people, not just the privileged and elite (e.g., the Sons of Liberty and the four Annapolis signers of the Declaration of Independence). In the museum, Braceli, with the help of a team of fabricators, created three enormous murals and two other works. The murals perform an autopsy of the tree. The largest multiplies the tulip poplar's distinctive leaf shape across a 33'-long wall in a wind-swept swirl of energy (the leaves were made from stencils of the Liberty Tree scion's actual leaves). A second mural abstracts the tree's tangled root system into a water-bearing drawing (using PVC tubing) that sprouts purple carnations. The third mural's subject is the tree's massive trunk, which was cut to pieces in 1999, with much of the wood later finding commemorative as Liberty Tree guitars, conference tables, and bible boxes. Onto nine chalkboards, Braceli has mounted nine pieces of raw wood, each supporting live orchids. What can we learn anew from this tree?, it seems to ask. The two other works urge us to turn away from nation-state identities and to look and listen more closely to nature. A sculptural ear is mounted onto the red silhouette of a rose petal, borrowed from the work of Columbia-born, Venezuela-based artist Roberto Obregoń. Nearby, a flag of yellow roses hangs from a flagpole that has been fabricated from a branch. Admission & Hours Free & open to the public Wednesday, Thursday, Saturday, and Sunday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Open Friday, 12 to 7:30 p.m. Parking

events.title: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power
events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

The exhibit will run from September 30th through October 28th, with a First Friday opening on October 2nd from 5-8pm. Reimagined marks a period of transition in Lori Niland Rounds’ artistic practice – one shaped by interruption, adaptation, and a changing way of seeing. Faced with an unexpected challenge that made familiar methods of working more difficult, Rounds began to reconsider both process and possibility. What initially felt like constraint gradually opened a different path forward, inviting experimentation with new gestures, materials, and ways of making. Richard Svec shares a mini-solo exhibit in the Lounge Gallery and Resident Artists exhibit new work in the Gallery Hall. Enjoy the sculptural work of Francis Maduka Uduh in studio 11, along with nineteen Gallery 209 Member Artists exhibiting their latest work. events.title: Shifting Boundaries: Perspectives on American Landscapes
events.address: Jefferson Drive at 12th St., SW, Washington, DC
events.description: American painters Willard Metcalf, Dwight Tryon, Winslow Homer, and Abbott Thayer created profoundly beautiful views of the New England landscapes where they lived and worked. These paintings largely depict that environment as timeless and static. Shifting Boundaries looks at these works from a new angle by engaging a multiplicity of voices and viewpoints to explore what these paintings can tell us about changes to this region both past and present. As Shifting Boundaries reveals, the views these artists created of pasturelands in Massachusetts and of seascapes in Maine were transforming even as these artists recorded them. This reshaping of landscapes has only accelerated in the century since Metcalf, Tryon, Homer, and Thayer depicted them. Shifting Boundaries pilots a new mode of collaborative curatorial practice. NMAA Lunder Curator of American Art Diana Greenwold , curatorial assistant Mary Mulcahy , and interpretation specialists Liz Gardner and Amy Freesun partnered with Lauren Brandes (Smithsonian Gardens), Dennis Chestnut (Groundwork Anacostia River DC), Jerome Foster II (Waic Up), Elizabeth James-Perry (Aquinnah Wampanoag artist), Lorette Picciano (Rural Coalition), Stephanie Toothman (National Park Service), and Melinda Whicher (Smithsonian Gardens) to develop the themes for this exhibition, select works of art, and write object labels. The group’s perspectives, drawn from their individual areas of professional expertise and their own personal experiences, allow us to see new details in these stunning works of art. The landscapes become invitations to explore a century of human impact on New England land and water, the erasure of indigenous histories, and the environmental changes that are altering this region today.

events.title: The American Story
events.description: The National Archives Museum debuts a once-in-a generation redesign of its permanent exhibits: The American Story and the Discovery Center - connecting visitors with the National Archives in revolutionary ways. The American Story will showcase items and records in the National Archives that tell important moments in our nation's history. Visitors will get up close to more than 40 original artifacts and documents, including a rare 1823 Stone Engraving of the Declaration of Independence, George Washington's annotated copy of the Constitution, and presidential gifts including horseshoes to President Bush from Queen Elizabeth II. The American Story will be the first and only museum in Washington, DC to use artificial intelligence (AI) to bring each visitor a special, individualized opportunity to explore the records of the American people and engage with American history. This exhibit brings more than two million historic records to life, offering a personalized journey through our nation's past. This new museum experience provides all Americans with a special opportunity to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence.

events.title: The Legend of Sleepy Hollow-Olney Theatre
events.description: Olney audiences were blown away in 2025, when we invited Synetic Theater to perform their award-winning, wordless version of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream . Now they’re back, but this time they’re tackling a story with classic American roots in the intimate confines of Olney Theatre Center’s 150-seat Theatre Lab. In the haunted village of Sleepy Hollow, the past refuses to stay buried. Years after a brutal Revolutionary War encounter leaves a Hessian soldier beheaded and his beloved horse slain, the fallen rider returns as the legendary Headless Horseman—an apparition stalking the shadowed forests in search of what was taken from him. Inspired by Washington Irving’s classic tale, Sleepy Hollow reimagines the familiar legend as a haunting story of love, guilt, revenge, and redemption. Blending supernatural horror with theatrical spectacle, it asks whether the true monsters are the spirits who haunt us—or the deeds we would rather forget. By Washington Irving Adapted by Nathan Weinberger Directed by Paata Tsikurishvili Choreographed by Irina Tsikurishvili Due to the layout of the Mulitz-Gudelsky Theatre Lab, late seating is at the discretion of the House Manager. Those exiting the theatre during the performance will not be re-admitted while the performance is in progress.

events.title: We Make History
events.description: As the nation commemorates 250 years since the signing of the Declaration of Independence, "We Make History" explores how history happens, is preserved and shared. In Washington, D.C. and places around the country, many people were quietly keeping the records, building the collections, and developing the skills that would create America’s historical narrative. These community-based stories serve as the building blocks for 250 years of American history. Using the country’s anniversary as a milestone, the museum uses its community driven practice to celebrate local civic engagement and encourage local history keeping. This exhibition is a tribute to celebrating our communities and making possible a better understanding of our shared past. These stories are important to marking the Semiquincentennial because they help show the legacy of how people make history one act, one document, one story at a time. By bringing these stories to the forefront in 2026, the exhibit inspires the next generation to keep and share their own stories and records to add to America’s historical narrative. We Make History has an anticipated opening date of May 30, 2026.

events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. events.title: Accelerating Authoritarianism:  Defending the Constitution Ahead of the Midterms
events.description: Authoritarianism Is Accelerating. The Midterms Are Coming. Here’s What You Can Do. Steven Cash, Executive Director of The Steady State Project, joins George Washington University Democracy Matters to discuss how to protect American democracy before the upcoming midterm elections. Authoritarianism in American government is accelerating, and the upcoming midterm elections may be one of the most important opportunities to push back. In this conversation, Steven Cash, the Executive Director of The Steady State, will explain what is at stake and what students and community members can do in the weeks leading up to Election Day. Whether you are already politically active or just starting to pay attention, you will leave with practical steps you can take right away. The guest speaker is Steven Cash, Executive Director of The Steady State, a former CIA operations officer, DHS senior intelligence official, and Senate counsel who helped draft post-9/11 national security legislation.

events.title: An Evening with ACOUSTIC ALCHEMY – RESCHEDULED TO APRIL 6, 2027!
Annapolis Witches & Legends Walking Tour
events.description: Take a walk through the history of Maryland's witch trials, superstition, and local legends with Annapolis Ghost Tours. Between the 1600s and 1700s, Maryland saw at least twelve witch trials. The last one was a capital case held right here in Annapolis. Several women in the colony were killed under suspicion of witchcraft, one was legally executed, and the stories of others have become legends that persist to this day. On this 90-minute walking tour, we will talk about the superstitions and accusations through the lens of local history.

events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. Image: Boris Ignatovich (Russian, 1899-1976), Composer Dmitri Shostakovich, from "Ignatovich, Soviet Avant-Garde", 1928, gelatin silver print, 16 H x 20 W in. events.title: Crossing the Red Line: Biden, His Advisors, and Israel's War in Gaza
events.description: The Middle East Policy Forum will host award-winning foreign affairs journalist Akbar Shahid Ahmed, author of Crossing the Red Line: Biden, His Advisors, and Israel's War in Gaza, on Wednesday, October 28. In a discussion moderated by Professor Marc Lynch, Ahmed will offer his powerful and authoritative account of how the Biden administration fueled atrocities in Gaza. In vivid prose and with unparalleled access to insiders, Ahmed depicts a White House that resisted a course correction as its failures became undeniable. He probes Biden’s inner circle, whose choices fueled tens of thousands of avoidable deaths among Palestinians, Lebanese, and Israelis, torpedoed long-time standards for warfare, and created a more dangerous world for us all. The Biden administration’s decisions drove voter backlash that helped Donald Trump regain power, and established patterns of impunity that have spurred wider bloodshed under Trump. Crossing the Red Line is an urgent reckoning with Biden’s record on Gaza that is vital to understanding historic damage to America’s standing in the world, and a period whose dark consequences will resonate globally for decades to come. We hope you will join the Middle East Policy Forum to hear from Akbar Shahid Ahmed about his new book. This event is open to the general public and media. events.description: The Chadwick A. This session, Research and Scholarship: Building and Sustaining a Scholarly Agenda, will explore practical strategies for developing a coherent and sustainable research agenda, with an emphasis on scholarly writing, publishing, and academic research. events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

Dr. Boutte is an accomplished pharmacy leader with extensive experience in pharmacy advocacy, health care policy, reimbursement, regulatory affairs and pharmacy practice. Her career includes leadership and professional roles with NACDS, Cigna HealthCare, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, CVS, Walgreens, Rite Aid and Walmart. Students will have the opportunity to learn about her career journey, the evolving role of pharmacists in health care and the importance of advocacy in advancing the profession.

events.description: Join us this October to celebrate Alfred Hitchcock, the master who gave us some of the most suspenseful moments in film history! STRANGERS ON A TRAIN October 7 at 4:00 and 7:00 Guy Haines wants a divorce. Bruno Antony wants his father dead. When the two meet aboard a train, Bruno proposes a solution to both their problems: he will murder Guy’s wife and Guy will murder Bruno’s father, leaving two victims and no motives. REAR WINDOW October 14 at 4:00 and 7:00 A newspaper photographer (James Stewart) with a broken leg passes time by observing his neighbors through his window. One evening, he sees what he believes to be a murder and decides to solve the crime himself, with the help of his nurse and his girlfriend (Grace Kelly). SUSPICION October 21 at 4:00 and 7:00 After eloping with a charming playboy (Cary Grant), Lina McLaidlaw (Joan Fontaine) soon discovers his gambling vice and mounting debts. As his lies deepen and those around him meet mysterious ends, Lina begins to suspect that her husband’s affection may conceal a deadly motive— and that she could be his next victim. VERTIGO October 28 at 4:00 and 7:00 Retired San Francisco police detective Scottie Ferguson (James Stewart) wrestles with his personal demons as he finds himself becoming obsessed with the beautiful woman (Kim Novak) he has been hired to trail, whose husband believes she is possessed. PSYCHO October 31 at 4:00 and 7:00 When Marion Crane (Janet Leigh) ends up at the Bates Motel after making off with $40,000 cash, there's hardly a film fan alive who doesn't know what happens next. It wouldn't be Hitchcocktober without his biggest hit!

events.title: Korea Policy Forum with Virginia Delegate Irene Shin
events.address: Elliott School of International Affairs, 1957 E ST NW, Washington DC 20052
events.description: Strengthening the U.S.-ROK Partnership Beyond Washington: The Growing Role of State and Local Leadership Virginia Delegate Irene Shin will discuss the increasingly influential role of state and local governments in the U.S.–ROK relationship. She will highlight the growing partnerships that states and localities have developed beyond federal-level diplomacy, particularly in areas of shared economic and cultural interests. As bilateral cooperation expands into investment, trade, education, and community engagement, state and local leaders are playing an important role in strengthening ties between the two countries. The discussion will explore the opportunities and challenges of building these connections and their implications for the future of the U.S.–ROK partnership. The GW Institute for Korean Studies invites you to join this timely discussion on the evolving role of state and local leadership in U.S.–ROK relations.

events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

events.title: Opening Reception: FOR FREEDOMS Exhibition
events.description: Bringing together two exhibitions — one tracing the legacy of Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT and Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY — the opening considers how artists take risks, mobilize collective action, and invites people into participatory experience. Three making stations extend the artists’ inquiries into shared practice. Visitors are invited to create mirror shields in solidarity with water protectors, make clay beads representing the wild bison population in America as part of Census, or respond to banned books, suppressed texts, and contested images through collage, image-making, and other forms of reinterpretation. Together, the exhibitions foreground artistic practice as a form of public courage: confronting censorship, environmental violence, and cultural erasure while building collective possibility. By placing participation at the center of the opening, the evening positions making as a civic act shaped through solidarity, exchange, and collective imagination.

events.description: Step into the shadowy world of The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari , the groundbreaking German silent horror film that forever changed the language of cinema. STARS: Conrad Veidt, Werner Krauss, Friedrich Feher RUNTIME: 51 Minutes GENRE: Silent Film, Film Noir, Psychological Horror, Mystery, Thriller RATING: PG-13 This show is part of the Silent Film Series , celebrating timeless scores and classic films. When the lights go down and the Mighty Wurlitzer rises from the orchestra pit, audiences are treated to a live organ performance featuring Tedde Gibson—complete with a short musical set before the credits roll and a brief introduction to each silent film. Our beloved Wurlitzer turns 100 this December, having filled the theater with music for nearly a century. The Weinberg Center , located in the heart of Downtown Frederick, MD, offers a historic backdrop for a unique film experience.

events.title: The Data Exorcist: Turning Metadata Nightmares into Tidy Data
events.description: Bad metadata can be downright frightening. In this hands-on workshop, you'll diagnose terrifying examples of poorly organized research metadata and learn practical skills for creating metadata that humans and computers can both work with. Along the way, you'll discover how thoughtful metadata organization improves reproducibility, reduces errors, and saves future-you (and your collaborators) from data horror stories. If you need personalized assistance with a data analysis, programming, or a coding project, consider booking a consultation with one of our librarian-experts. Learn more about our services to support programming and coding and for working with data. All sessions are free to GW students, faculty, staff, and alumni. GW has an institutional commitment to ensuring that all of our programs and events are accessible for all individuals. If you require any accommodations to participate in this event, please contact libraryevents@gwu.edu at least 72 business hours (3 business days) prior to the event.

events.title: The Legend of Sleepy Hollow-Olney Theatre
events.description: Olney audiences were blown away in 2025, when we invited Synetic Theater to perform their award-winning, wordless version of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream . Now they’re back, but this time they’re tackling a story with classic American roots in the intimate confines of Olney Theatre Center’s 150-seat Theatre Lab. In the haunted village of Sleepy Hollow, the past refuses to stay buried. Years after a brutal Revolutionary War encounter leaves a Hessian soldier beheaded and his beloved horse slain, the fallen rider returns as the legendary Headless Horseman—an apparition stalking the shadowed forests in search of what was taken from him. Inspired by Washington Irving’s classic tale, Sleepy Hollow reimagines the familiar legend as a haunting story of love, guilt, revenge, and redemption. Blending supernatural horror with theatrical spectacle, it asks whether the true monsters are the spirits who haunt us—or the deeds we would rather forget. By Washington Irving Adapted by Nathan Weinberger Directed by Paata Tsikurishvili Choreographed by Irina Tsikurishvili Due to the layout of the Mulitz-Gudelsky Theatre Lab, late seating is at the discretion of the House Manager. Those exiting the theatre during the performance will not be re-admitted while the performance is in progress.

events.title: Ukraine–Hungary Relations: A New Chapter?
events.description: Well into its fifth year of all-out war, Ukraine has faced unexpectedly tense relations with some of its neighbors, potentially jeopardizing Ukraine's EU aspirations, despite strong shared interests in resisting Russian aggression. The Petrach Program on Ukraine is thus launching a series of discussions on developments between Ukraine and its neighbors. This first event in the series focuses on Hungary, where Kyiv's longtime nemesis and Putin ally, Viktor Orban, was recently ousted. Moderated by a leading scholar of Eastern European politics, three specialists on Hungary and Ukraine will examine what has changed in Hungary and what has not, assess a recent Ukrainian law on education and language that Hungary has demanded for Ukraine's ethnic Hungarian population, and consider whether a full reconciliation between the two countries is now possible.

events.title: Unfossilizing African Art
events.description: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. Image: Once Known Mende carver [Mende, Sierra Leone], Sowei, 19th-20th century, wood, varnish, 16 H x 10 W x 10 D in. Gift of Stephen A. Spear, 1975 (P.75.2.30)

events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. events.title: Afro-Cuban All Stars
events.description: Afro-Cuban All Stars is a multigenerational orchestra devoted to promoting the full range of Cuban music, bringing together musicians across styles and eras. Led by bandleader Juan de Marcos González—also a central figure in the Buena Vista Social Club project—the ensemble reflects a long-standing approach rooted in tradition while embracing contemporary Cuban sounds. Their program moves across son, bolero, and rhythm-driven dance styles, drawing on the musical traditions of Cuba’s mid-20th-century golden age. Founded in the 1990s, the group continues to evolve through a flexible lineup that incorporates younger musicians alongside established artists. More than a fixed ensemble, Afro-Cuban All Stars operates as a shifting orchestra, adapting its sound to reflect different periods and styles, grounded in González’s concept of building on musical roots while creating space for the future.

The exhibition will highlight six Maryland insect species that are included on Maryland’s List of Rare, Threatened, and Endangered Animals . events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Charlene Kaye: Diversity Shredder
events.description: Welcome to the unhinged, razor-sharp, fluorescent universe of Charlene Kaye: guitar god, internet legend and “breakout comedy star” according to Rolling Stone. Known for her countless viral videos such as “Every Taylor Swift Song” (100M views and counting), she brings us a brand new Diversity Shredder! Kaye has been touring her critically acclaimed debut show "Tiger Daughter: Or, How I Brought My Immigrant Mother Ultimate Shame," presented by comedy icon Margaret Cho. That show played to sold-out runs at Edinburgh Fringe 2024 and Melbourne International Comedy Festival 2025, and it will soon be filmed as her first comedy special. While Tiger Daughter was a hilarious and heartfelt hour about her mother, Diversity Shredder is a madcap musical about being a menace to society as an Asian woman guitar shredder. From starting out as a folk singer-songwriter, to shredding in wizard rock band Team StarKid, to starting endless gender-flipped cover bands like Guns N’ Hoses and Labiahead, it’s an unhinged tour of her musical universe. You’ll be rolling in your seats, you’ll learn a lot about how music works, and you might even confuse her for Bobby Lee. Anything is possible!

events.title: Claiming the Sea: Asian Perspectives on Maritime Dominance
events.description: Asia’s seas have long served as arenas of commerce, cooperation, contestation, and conflict. Today, the maritime expanse stretching from the Indian Ocean to the Arctic stands at the center of global geopolitics, economic flows, environmental pressures, and strategic competition—military, legal, and otherwise. With these dynamics in mind, this conference seeks to foster interdisciplinary dialogue on how maritime dominance is conceptualized, pursued, and contested across Asian contexts. events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

events.title: Hermit Day
events.description: Hermit Day October 29 @ 9:30 am - 4:00 pm Day of Quiet at Bon Secours Do you… need a day of quiet and solitude to rest, reflect, be? need at least one of these each year? sense that God may be inviting you to enter silence and reorient? October 29 th might be just for you, as it is the annual celebration of National Hermit Day. Although its origins are not firmly known, many attribute Hermit Day’s origin to the 18th century and suggest a connection to the Irish Hermit Saint Colman. It gives us an opportunity to join the many others who — throughout Christian history — have entered silence and solitude to remember what is most important: to listen, to pray. A day like this has the potential to initiate or strengthen a regular practice. Since 2014, Bon Secours Retreat and Conference Center has hosted Quiet Morning events that are also opportunities for shared silence. This day will follow a similar pattern. We will begin and end together in simple prayer, have lunch in shared silence, and spend the day on our own in prayer or other quiet activities such as walking, doing art, reading, journaling — whatever you feel inclined to do. The Center’s daily Mass at 11:00 am will be available to you, if desired. This is mostly a silent retreat. Lunch is included. Guided by Joanne Cahoon.

events.title: Making Meaning in the Modern World
events.description: Our well-being grows when we create, when we connect, and when we know that we matter to other people. Decades of research and thousands of human stories tell us that making and mattering are powerful antidotes to overwhelm and disconnection. Join New York Times bestselling authors Kelly Corrigan (The Middle Place and Tell Me More) and Jennifer Wallace (Never Enough and Mattering) for a conversation about making, mattering, and the simple things that help us build meaningful lives. Drawing from Corrigan’s exploration of creativity and making, and Wallace’s analysis and collection of research on the science of mattering, the evening weaves together personal stories and practical wisdom to explore what helps people flourish. The event features individual talks from each author and an on-stage conversation between the authors and local educators. Come celebrate the simple but powerful idea that the lives we build together are shaped by both what we make and by knowing that we matter. This event is supported by the Walton Family Foundation.

events.title: Maryland Witches Pub Crawl
events.description: The Witches of Maryland Pub Crawl is a tour through the history of witch trials, accusations, superstitions, and legends. Sip on a beverage while entertained by stories of suspicion, fear, and the women whose names were tied to witchcraft in Annapolis and across Maryland. Your guide will bring to life the legends, trials, and lore that shaped our colonial past. The Witches of Maryland Pub Crawl is a 2-hour pub crawl (approx. ½ mile) into some of the storied taverns of Annapolis. Spending about 20–30 minutes at each location, you’ll relax with a cocktail while learning about the accusations, trials, and superstitions that spread through Maryland — and the lasting stories that have become part of our local history. We will visit three bars on each crawl — locations visited may include some of the following: 🍸 Drinks are not included in this tour. This tour is limited to Adults (21+) ONLY! No children. show less

events.title: Mental Reset: Sound Bath + Reiki : Thursday Evenings in Falls Church
events.address: 7777 Leesburg Pike, Ste 204S, Falls Church, VA 22043
events.description: Thursday is a weird day. The week isn't over, but you are. Mental Reset is one hour at the end of the workday where nobody needs anything from you. You come in, you lie down on a mat, you get a blanket and a bolster, and for the next sixty minutes your only job is to listen. I play crystal singing bowls, guide you through a short meditation so your mind has something to do besides replay the day, and offer Reiki while you rest. Most people tell me some version of the same thing afterward: the noise in their head finally turned down. Not off: down. Enough that they can go home and actually be home, instead of answering emails in their head at the dinner table. You don't need experience. You don't need to know how to meditate, and you definitely don't need to “clear your mind.” If you could do that, you wouldn't need this class. First-timers are in the room most weeks. There are ten spots. That's deliberate. It's a small room, I can see everyone in it, and it never feels like an event. It feels like an exhale. A few regulars started as skeptics; more than one of our Google reviews comes from someone who arrived doubting the whole thing and left surprised at how settled they felt. You don't have to believe in anything for an hour of sound and rest to do you some good. Run by Victoria Vita: CPA for 20+ years, healer for 7+. I sat behind a desk with a brain that wouldn't switch off for a long time before I found this work. Thursday nights are built for the person I used to be. Rated 5.0 from 32 Google reviews. Come straight from work. Leave like the week let go of you first. What's included: • 60 minutes of crystal singing bowls, guided meditation and Reiki • Mat, blanket, and bolster everything is here; you bring nothing • Small group: 10 people maximum, same teacher every week • Time at the end to sit up slowly, have water, and not rush out Discover More Attractions in #FXVA

events.title: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power
events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

events.title: Research & Enrichment! Science with Your Dog
events.description: Join the GW Dog Lab for fun, free enrichment with your dog! The GW Canine Cognition Collaborative (aka GW Dog Lab) is a student-run lab in the Anthropology Department. Research sessions are on campus, after hours and on weekends, and are designed to last only 1 hour. Because humans and dogs share an environment, we can learn a lot about the way that environment has shaped our species by comparing dog and toddler cognition. We play simple games with dogs designed to measure their cognition and then compare them to toddlers. How to Participate 1. Start by submitting a pre-screening form. This helps us learn about your dog 2. Next, open your email and look for your onboarding information sent from canine.cognition@gwu.edu. 3. Then, using the information in your email, sign up for your initial visit. This is a get-to-know-you visit that makes it easier for dogs to get acclimated to our testing space. 4. Finally, after the initial visit, depending on your dog's comfort level, you will get email invitations to studies your dog is eligible for! Parking information can be found on the GW Dog Lab website.

events.title: The Legend of Sleepy Hollow-Olney Theatre
events.description: Olney audiences were blown away in 2025, when we invited Synetic Theater to perform their award-winning, wordless version of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream . Now they’re back, but this time they’re tackling a story with classic American roots in the intimate confines of Olney Theatre Center’s 150-seat Theatre Lab. In the haunted village of Sleepy Hollow, the past refuses to stay buried. Years after a brutal Revolutionary War encounter leaves a Hessian soldier beheaded and his beloved horse slain, the fallen rider returns as the legendary Headless Horseman—an apparition stalking the shadowed forests in search of what was taken from him. Inspired by Washington Irving’s classic tale, Sleepy Hollow reimagines the familiar legend as a haunting story of love, guilt, revenge, and redemption. Blending supernatural horror with theatrical spectacle, it asks whether the true monsters are the spirits who haunt us—or the deeds we would rather forget. By Washington Irving Adapted by Nathan Weinberger Directed by Paata Tsikurishvili Choreographed by Irina Tsikurishvili Due to the layout of the Mulitz-Gudelsky Theatre Lab, late seating is at the discretion of the House Manager. Those exiting the theatre during the performance will not be re-admitted while the performance is in progress.

events.title: The Unfinished America: A 250-Year Journey of Liberty and Economic Freedom
events.description: Meet at the World War II Kiosk and join a National Park Service volunteer for an immersive 90-minute walking tour exploring the evolution of individual liberty and economic freedom while visiting several National Mall monuments and memorials. From the towering legacy of George Washington to the revolutionary courage of the 56 Signers of the Declaration of Independence, we will trace America’s fitful yet persistent progress toward a "more perfect union." This journey weaves together iconic sites with personal stories of stowaways, soldiers, and the "Greatest Generation" to honor the sacrifices that built our modern world. As we celebrate this year's historic semiquincentennial, you are invited to connect your own family’s legacy to our shared pursuit of freedom and learn about nationwide celebrations ahead. Discover why the torch lit 250 years ago remains an exceptional beacon of democratic leadership in the world today. Memorials visited include: WWII and Washington Monument, Japanese Lantern, Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial, Korean and Vietnam War Memorials, the Lincoln Memorial, and Signers' Island.

events.title: Truth Over Power: A Center for Journalism & Democracy Speaker Series
events.description: Two of the nation’s most fearless voices. One defining moment for American democracy. A conversation at the Mecca. Her reporting has helped shape a generation's understanding of American history. Ta-Nehisi Coates, is the author of the No. 1 New York Times bestseller Between the World and Me, winner of the 2015 National Book Award for Nonfiction. He is also the author of the bestselling books The Beautiful Struggle, We Were Eight Years in Power, and The Water Dancer. His numerous books, articles and essays have challenged America to reckon honestly with itself. Together, Hannah-Jones and Coates, whose works have been the target of widespread bans across the nation, will help contextualize this unprecedented moment ahead of an election that will determine whether American democracy will hold. Kimberly R. Moffitt, Dean of the Cathy Hughes School of Communications at Howard University, will moderate the conversation. Digital only tickets are still available for the Truth Over Power Speaker Series on Oct. 29. Register now to have a recording of the conversation sent to you via email. events.title: Unfossilizing African Art
events.description: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. Image: Once Known Mende carver [Mende, Sierra Leone], Sowei, 19th-20th century, wood, varnish, 16 H x 10 W x 10 D in. Gift of Stephen A. Spear, 1975 (P.75.2.30)

events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. events.title: Another Look, Another World (Insect Art) Exhibition
events.description: An art-science exhibition about Maryland's insect diversity and insect conservation. Tue Oct 27 9:00am To – 5:00pm Parren J. Mitchell Art-Sociology Building Another Look, Another World Exhibition Web Page Another Look, Another World Exhibition Web Page Add to Calendar Another Look, Another World is an interdisciplinary exhibition exploring how visual art may deepen our understanding of Maryland’s insect biodiversity and inspire greater appreciation for the ecological roles insects play in our environment. The exhibition is part of a University of Maryland Arts for All-funded project aimed at engaging students in science communication through art, increasing awareness of insect biodiversity and ecological roles, fostering collaboration across disciplines, evaluating changes in attendee knowledge, attitudes, and intentions, and contributing to a replicable arts-based model for conservation education. The exhibition will highlight six Maryland insect species that are included on Maryland’s List of Rare, Threatened, and Endangered Animals . Original works created through the exhibition’s two different open calls will be displayed alongside science-based information about insect ecological roles, insect habitats, and key conservation actions. events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. Image: Boris Ignatovich (Russian, 1899-1976), Composer Dmitri Shostakovich, from "Ignatovich, Soviet Avant-Garde", 1928, gelatin silver print, 16 H x 20 W in. events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

events.title: Is There Room for Revolutionary Conservatives in a Liberal Democracy? Lessons from the U.S. and Poland
events.description: In old and new democracies alike, the right has largely given up its traditional instinct to conserve. Instead, it has adopted the revolutionary tactics once associated with the Left. The United States (Donald Trump case) and Poland (Law & Justice—PiS case) are the two clearest cases in which this “conservative revolution” has gone full circle—seizing power, losing it, refusing to disappear, and then returning—all while holding on to somewhere between a third and a half of the electorate. The recent Oxford University Press volume Let’s Agree on Poland (eds. Maciej Kisilowski and Anna Wojciuk, 2025) confronts precisely the problems that follow from this situation, and forms the basis for this event. The event has four aims. The first is to introduce a U.S. policy, academic, and student audience to the “conservative revolutionaries” framework and to the Polish debate over a new social contract and the need for a new constitutional design. The second is to compare the Polish and American cycles of conservative revolution and liberal counter-revolution—the fights over courts, public media, the politics of prosecution, and contested transfers of power. The third is to ask whether institutional accommodation—federalism, decentralization, a vertical division of power—offers a realistic alternative to winner-takes-all politics in both countries. events.title: Join Historic Annapolis: Very Superstitious! Paca House and Garden Tour: A History of Luck, Lore, and Beliefs
events.description: Discover the fascinating world of superstitions, folklore, and everyday beliefs that shaped life in centuries past. On this guided tour of the William Paca House and Garden, explore the origins of customs and practices once accepted as fact and, in some cases, still observed today. From household rituals to good-luck charms and protective practices, uncover the meanings behind these enduring traditions and learn how they influenced daily life. Join us for an engaging journey into the beliefs that helped people make sense of an uncertain world and discover how echoes of these old superstitions still linger today. At the conclusion of the tour, guests are invited to enjoy seasonal refreshments and share their favorite superstition! Note: This tour will be offered on a range of dates and times in October. To see times, visit our October event calendar . Cost: $15 General Admission. $12 for Historic Annapolis members and Military. Weather or private events may alter the tour route. Please dress for the weather. Advance registration recommended; space is limited. Interested in a private version of this tour for your group of 10 or more? events.title: Legends & Lore
events.description: Come see the darker side of Frederick. When night falls, Frederick’s familiar streets have rather different stories to tell. Climb aboard our vintage double-decker for an hour of dark tales from Frederick’s past , researched from local histories, old accounts and the legends that have lingered long after the people involved have gone. As we make our way through the city, we’ll slow down at the very places connected to these stories, from historic streets and old buildings to some of Frederick’s more famously haunted places . Along the way, you’ll hear tales of strange happenings, restless spirits and the darker chapters of local history, all told against the backdrop of Frederick after dark. And because it’s October, you’ll also get a rather good view from the top deck as the city’s historic homes and neighborhoods put on their best autumn and Halloween displays. Whether you’re a believer, a skeptic, or simply enjoy a good story with a slightly unsettling ending, Legends and Lore offers a different way to discover Frederick’s history. Just remember, it’s much easier to laugh at a ghost story when you’re not sitting on the top deck in the dark. TOUR HIGHLIGHTS Hear researched tales of Frederick’s haunted places, local legends and darker history, told where the stories happened. Experience Frederick after dark from the top deck, with historic streets, autumn displays and a few places you’ll look at rather differently afterwards. TOUR DETAILS Price: $35 per person Duration: 1 hour Recommended Age: 14+ Departure: RAK Brewing Co, 400 Sagner Ave, Frederick, MD, 21701

events.title: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power
events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

events.title: OneGW Summit: Many Voices. OneGW.
events.description: We are at a pivotal point in our university's history, with opportunities to build our institution’s future. In alignment with the Strategic Framework, and inspired by principles of an inclusive community - derived from scholars, researchers, activists, changemakers, youth, and organizers - we bring the GW community our 11th OneGW Summit: Many Voices. OneGW. Across three transformative days, our university will host students, faculty, staff, alumni, and community members to confront the hard questions about community building and chart a bolder path forward. We will challenge comfortable narratives about higher education and identify frameworks that turn good intentions into measurable change. The Summit will: Host candid conversations on equity in the classroom and beyond, workshops that equip you with real tools for being in coalition and working across difference, and voices who bring to their leadership roles humility and the capacity to listen to all members of our communityServe as a catalyst for deeper engagement, connection, and meaningful dialogueHonor the coexistence of multiple truths, demonstrating our strength to come together, break bread, and build as OneGW. This is a GW experience where disagreement is welcome, where lived experience is data, and where every voice — especially those too often unheard — shapes deliberation and decision-making. events.title: Research & Enrichment! Science with Your Dog
events.description: Join the GW Dog Lab for fun, free enrichment with your dog! The GW Canine Cognition Collaborative (aka GW Dog Lab) is a student-run lab in the Anthropology Department. Research sessions are on campus, after hours and on weekends, and are designed to last only 1 hour. Because humans and dogs share an environment, we can learn a lot about the way that environment has shaped our species by comparing dog and toddler cognition. We play simple games with dogs designed to measure their cognition and then compare them to toddlers. How to Participate 1. Start by submitting a pre-screening form. This helps us learn about your dog 2. Next, open your email and look for your onboarding information sent from canine.cognition@gwu.edu. 3. Then, using the information in your email, sign up for your initial visit. This is a get-to-know-you visit that makes it easier for dogs to get acclimated to our testing space. 4. Finally, after the initial visit, depending on your dog's comfort level, you will get email invitations to studies your dog is eligible for! Parking information can be found on the GW Dog Lab website.

events.title: Spirits, Zombies, and Vampires in East Asia
events.description: Event Address: 1957 E Street, NW Room 212 Date: Friday, October 30, 2026 from 12:30-2:00 pm Contact us at rollielal@gwu.edu Please join the Global Affairs and Religion Network (GARNET) for this event with Dr. Xiaofei Kang on Ghosts and Witches in China and Dr. Rollie Lal on Spirits and Vampires in Japan. We will be discussing different and frightful perspectives on the afterlife in East Asia through the lens of popular fiction, film, and folklore. This event is co-sponsored by Security Policy Studies (SPS) and the Sigur Center for Asian Studies. The GARNET is a collegial conversation across the fields of religion and global affairs. The network brings together MA students from the Elliott School of International Affairs each month to discuss a topic that weaves religion and security. RSVP

events.title: The Legend of Sleepy Hollow-Olney Theatre
events.description: Olney audiences were blown away in 2025, when we invited Synetic Theater to perform their award-winning, wordless version of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream . Now they’re back, but this time they’re tackling a story with classic American roots in the intimate confines of Olney Theatre Center’s 150-seat Theatre Lab. In the haunted village of Sleepy Hollow, the past refuses to stay buried. Years after a brutal Revolutionary War encounter leaves a Hessian soldier beheaded and his beloved horse slain, the fallen rider returns as the legendary Headless Horseman—an apparition stalking the shadowed forests in search of what was taken from him. Inspired by Washington Irving’s classic tale, Sleepy Hollow reimagines the familiar legend as a haunting story of love, guilt, revenge, and redemption. Blending supernatural horror with theatrical spectacle, it asks whether the true monsters are the spirits who haunt us—or the deeds we would rather forget. By Washington Irving Adapted by Nathan Weinberger Directed by Paata Tsikurishvili Choreographed by Irina Tsikurishvili Due to the layout of the Mulitz-Gudelsky Theatre Lab, late seating is at the discretion of the House Manager. events.title: Unfossilizing African Art
events.description: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. Image: Once Known Mende carver [Mende, Sierra Leone], Sowei, 19th-20th century, wood, varnish, 16 H x 10 W x 10 D in. Gift of Stephen A. Spear, 1975 (P.75.2.30)

events.title: "MCP Servers Are a New Attack Surface: How to Securely Build and Use Them" at BSides Northern Virginia
events.venue: George Mason University Schar School of Policy and Government
events.description: Hear from GW Engineering alumnus Saquib Saifee, M.S. '23, Security Engineer at IBM, CISSP, eCPPT, at BSides Northern Virginia in Arlington, VA! On October 31, he will present "MCP Servers Are a New Attack Surface: How to Securely Build and Use Them" to an engaged audience of security engineers and AI practitioners. Model Context Protocol (MCP) is only as secure as the server you build it on. In under two years, it has become the standard integration layer connecting AI agents to enterprise systems, databases, source code, and production APIs. However, an agent crosses a trust boundary on every tool call and resource fetch, and the protocol leaves the server to decide what is allowed. If the server does not enforce those boundaries, nothing else will. Grounded in real-world incidents and contributions to the OWASP GenAI Security Project, this practitioner-focused talk provides an actionable builder’s guide to securing MCP architectures. events.title: A Dose of Dupas Presents: The Poetry Takeover Brunch
A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think.
